where: Section 1, the short-dipole formula, and Worked example 1 steps 2 and 4
problem: The chapter says a short dipole's current falls to zero at the tips, then quotes Rr = 80π²(l/λ)². That value assumes a uniform (constant) current along the dipole. For a real short dipole with the triangular current distribution the chapter itself describes, referred to the current maximum, the value is Rr = 20π²(l/λ)² — one quarter of what is quoted. The table entries (8 Ω at λ/10, 0.32 Ω at λ/50) and the worked example results all rest on the unstated uniform-current assumption, so a student cannot tell which convention applies.
fix: State the assumption explicitly. Uniform-current (infinitesimal) dipole: Rr = 80π²(l/λ)² referred to the terminal current. Real short dipole with triangular current, referred to the current maximum: Rr = 20π²(l/λ)², i.e. 2 Ω at λ/10 and 0.08 Ω at λ/50. If the triangular value is used, Example 1 becomes Rr = 20π²(0.05)² = 0.49 Ω, RA = 0.99 Ω and ηrad = 0.49/0.99 ≈ 0.50, not 0.80.

problem: The lead says "An antenna has three numbers that decide how well it works", but the chapter treats four quantities: radiation resistance, efficiency, effective aperture and polarization.
fix: "Four quantities decide how well an antenna works." Or drop the count and name them.

where: Section 3, the half-wave dipole at 300 MHz
problem: "The metal itself is a few centimetres across" invites the wrong picture: a half-wave dipole at 300 MHz is about 0.5 m long, tip to tip. Only its wire thickness is a few millimetres.
fix: "…though the antenna is only a thin half-metre wire; the 0.13 m² is a capture area, not a physical size."

where: Exam traps, third bullet (peak versus rms current)
problem: "This gives a factor-of-two error in both Rr and efficiency" is not right for efficiency. A factor of two in Rr gives an efficiency error that depends on RL — with true Rr = 2 Ω and RL = 1 Ω, the wrong Rr = 1 Ω gives η = 0.5 instead of 0.667, not a factor of two.
fix: "This halves (or doubles) the computed Rr; the error it produces in the efficiency depends on how large RL is."

where: Section 2, "at l = λ/50 the same 0.5 Ω takes almost everything"
problem: "Almost everything" overstates it on the chapter's own numbers: 0.32 Ω against 0.5 Ω gives ηrad ≈ 0.39, so about 61 per cent is lost, not almost all.
fix: "…the same 0.5 Ω leaves an efficiency of only 0.32/(0.32+0.5) ≈ 0.39, so most of the input power heats the metal."

problem: "Radiation resistance grows as the square of electrical length" is only true in the very-short-dipole region; the λ/2 dipole at 73 Ω in the same table does not lie on that square-law curve, so the caption contradicts its own data.
fix: "Below about λ/10 the radiation resistance grows as the square of electrical length; by λ/2 it has reached 73 Ω and the square law no longer holds."
